XXXIII.5 September - October 2026
A Born-Accessible Approach to
Technology Design

text.tspan: Authors:
Jonathan Lazar, Kyle Shachmut, Andrew Drummond, Jay Wyant, Howard Rosenblum,
Katherine Eng
Digital technologies have become an integral part of our daily lives, shaping how we
communicate, learn, work, and interact with the world. Yet, for millions of people with
disabilities (PWD), these innovations often present barriers rather than opportunities.
Historically, software, electronic documents, web content, and other digital technologies
and content have been developed without fully considering the diverse needs and
preferences of PWD. This oversight has led to exclusion, frustration, and missed
opportunities both for individuals and organizations. Traditionally, accessibility has been
addressed reactively. Technologies are built, but organizations attempt to "fix"
accessibility barriers only after complaints and legal challenges are lodged [
]. This
remediation approach is costly, time-consuming, and often results in inferior user
experiences for PWD. Worse, it perpetuates exclusion and disfranchisement, compelling
individuals to advocate for and wait for fixes, which frequently never occur.
Insights
Born-accessible design embeds accessibility and the lived experience of
people with disabilities from the beginning, and throughout all stages, of
technology development.
Laws and policies are beginning to require born-accessible design, so the
HCI community needs to define methods, tools, and activities for such
design.
By embedding accessibility from the very beginning—through design,
development, and procurement—organizations can ensure that technology is
inclusive, efficient, and future-proof.
